region.en: Konya, shop of the oil-press (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞油坊（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887 (abridged), public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A parrot kept in the shop of an oilman speaks to the customers and drives away trade; the master threatens it, and the bird falls silent and shivers like a dead thing. The oilman carries it out and flings it on the dunghill. The bird rises on the wing, and the master learns that the parrot has taught the other parrots his own trade: silence is the one thing that cannot be talked about.
summary.zh: 油商鋪中一鸚鵡對客高談，趕走生意；主人威脅之，鳥遂默然顫抖如死物。油商攜之擲於糞堆。鳥振翅而起；主人方知鸚鵡已教眾鸚鵡他自己的營生：沉默乃無法言說之事。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: An oilman kept a parrot in his shop, a bird that could talk, and it talked the customers into and out of everything; trade went to ruin. The oilman threatened it, and the parrot fell silent and hung its head, and shivered, and made itself like a dead thing. The oilman grieved, and carried the bird out into the court, and flung it on the dunghill with the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Oilman and his Parrot'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The parrot rose from the dunghill on the wing, and flew to the garden, and sat among the parrots of the garden. And when the master saw it fly, he understood: the bird had made itself dead that it might go free, and it had gone to teach the garden-parrots the one trade it knew — to be silent, and so escape the talker's snare. The moral of the tale is the speechlessness of the lover of God, who must be nothing, that he may be all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

region.en: Wayside in the wilderness of Sinai (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西奈曠野路旁（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 2 (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 2

summary.en: A shepherd on the road praises God in shepherd's words: 'I will comb thy hair, I will milk thee, I will kiss thy hand.' Moses rebukes him: 'Thou hast joined to God what does not become Him.' The shepherd tears his garment and departs. A voice comes to Moses: 'Thou hast come to unite, not to sever — I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward spirit.' Moses runs after the shepherd, who has understood: 'To each his own form of worship.'
summary.zh: 牧羊人以牧人言辭讚主：『我要為你梳髮、擠奶、吻你之手。』穆薩斥之：『你以不當之物配主。』牧人撕裂其衣而去。有聲臨穆薩：『你來是為聯合，非為割裂——我不看言與語，我看內在之靈。』穆薩追上牧人，牧人已悟：『各有各的敬拜形式。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment; the tale's theology is the poet's own, not scripture.

passages.text: A shepherd saw Moses on the road and said, 'Where art thou going, beloved of God?' Moses said, 'To pray to God, that He may pardon our sins.' The shepherd said, 'I will pray with thee'; and he prayed in shepherd's words: 'O God, I will comb Thy hair and wash Thy garments and kiss Thy hand and milk Thee, and bring Thee to my tent.' Moses said, 'What babbling is this? Thou hast joined to God what does not become Him: milk, and a comb, and sandals!' The shepherd tore his garment, sighed, and fled into the desert.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 2, 'Moses and the Shepherd'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then came a revelation to Moses: 'Thou hast come to unite, and thou hast severed. I look not at the tongue and the speech; I look at the inward spirit and the state. What are courtesy and the canons of speech? The light of the heart is my desire. Thou art gone to the temple and the law; and he has gone to be intoxicated with the Beloved. Thy way is good, his way is good too.' And Moses ran after the shepherd, who understood at last: 'To each his own form of worship; the Sufi has no kite and quarry but God.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 2; not verbatim.

region.en: Konya, a dark house by night (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞夜間暗屋（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 3 (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 3

summary.en: An elephant is brought for show to a dark house; the visitors enter by a lamp each in turn and come out with different reports: a water-pipe, a fan, a pillar, a throne. They quarrel all night with candles in their hands. Had each held a candle, they had been one word short of truth — but each had only one lamp, and the elephant is only a figure of the Real, which each partial seer names after the part his hand has found.
summary.zh: 一象供觀賞置於暗屋；參觀者各持一燈輪流入，出而各異其辭：水管、扇、柱、御座。他們徹夜執燭相爭。若各持全燭，則離真理僅一詞——然每人只有一燈；象只是實在的比喻，各偏見者以手所觸之部分而名之。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: Some Hindoos were exhibiting an elephant, and all the people desired to see it; but the house was too dark, and so a lamp was provided, and the beholders went in one by one. In the dark they felt the beast with their hands, and each came out and gave a different report: one had found the trunk and cried 'A water-pipe!' another the ear and cried 'A fan!' another the leg and cried 'A pillar!' another the back and cried 'A throne!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, 'The Elephant in the Dark'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They quarrelled all night with candles in their hands, each calling the others liars. If each had held a candle, the discrepancy would have gone out of their words — for all would have seen the one elephant. And the tale is told, says Rumi, of the seers and sects, who each see one member of the Real in the dark of this world, and each name it after the part his hand has found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3; not verbatim.

title.en: The Travellers Who Ate the Young Elephant

region.zh: 印度曠野之路（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 3, Story I (composed c. 1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 3, Story I

summary.en: A party lost in the wilderness is starving; a sage shows them young elephants in the wood and warns them that the parents will track and avenge. They kill and eat one, and sleep; in the morning each has hidden in a different quarter, and the great elephants find them out one by one and trample them — every one, as the sage had said, except the man who told him where they were going.
summary.zh: 迷途之眾瀕餓；一智者示林中幼象，並警其父母必追而復仇。眾殺而食之一，睡去；晨間各匿不同方位，巨象逐一尋出踐踏——如智者所言，無一倖免，惟那位曾告訴智者去向者得免。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A party of travellers lost their way in a wilderness and were well-nigh famished. A sage came up and condoled with them, and told them there were many young elephants in the adjacent woods, one of which would furnish an ample meal; but he warned them that if they killed one, its parents would in all probability track them out and be revenged. They saw a plump young elephant, and could not resist killing and eating it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, Story I; not verbatim.

passages.text: They slept, and each, it is said, hid himself in a different quarter, and one told the sage where they meant to hide. In the morning the great elephants came, and went from hiding-place to hiding-place, and trampled them one by one, every man of them — as the sage had said; and only the man who had told him where they were going came off alive. The moral, says Rumi, is of the men who slay the young of the Lord's creatures and think their hiding from the elephant is hiding from God.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 3, Story I; not verbatim.

region.zh: 科尼亞屋頂羅網（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A fowler snares a little bird on a roof, and the bird sings three songs to ransom itself: the first from the snare, the second from the hand, the third from the heart of the fowler — 'Three counsels I give in the mouth of thy three gates.' The first: 'Regret not what is past.' The second: 'Do not believe impossibilities.' The third: 'A pearl of great price lies in thy own garden; do not dig beyond it.' And the bird, escaping, mocks him gently: the pearl is its own body, which the fowler held and let go.
summary.zh: 捕鳥者於屋頂網得一鳥；鳥唱三歌贖身：第一歌贖自羅網，第二贖自手中，第三贖自捕者之心——『我以三言付汝三門之口』。其一：『勿悔既往。』其二：『勿信不可能之事。』其三：『至寶之珠在汝園中；勿掘園外。』鳥脫逃後溫言相嘲：珠即其身——捕者曾握而放之。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A fowler caught a little bird in a snare on the roof, and would have killed it; and the bird spoke: 'What wilt thou do with me? I am not a mouthful.' And it said, 'I will give thee three counsels, if thou let me go: the first on thy fingers, the second at the gate, the third in the heart of the field.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Fowler and the Bird'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The first counsel, given on the fingers: 'Regret not what is past.' The second, given standing free: 'Do not believe impossibilities — believe not that a bird should weigh six ounces and be heavier than an elephant.' And the third, given as it flew from the tree: 'In thy belly are thirty paces of pearl; but beyond thy own garden do not dig.' And the fowler stood repenting of his greed, and the bird called out: 'The pearl is my little body, which thou didst hold and didst let go.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

region.en: Court of the qazi, Konya (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞法官法庭（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A qazi of the city judges by the letter; a wandering dervish is brought before him. The dervish tells the story of the jurist who slept with the light burning and demanded of the night why it had robbed him — and the tale turns the court's own grammar against it. The qazi is silent; the dervish goes; and the poem says the judge of the letter has never seen the day of the spirit.
summary.zh: 城中法官依字面而判；一行腳苦行僧被帶至其前。苦行僧講述一法官燃燈而眠、向夜索其被竊之光的故事——此喻反轉法庭自身之語法。法官默然；苦行僧離去；詩云字面之判者未嘗見靈之晝。

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A qazi judged by the letter of the law, and a wandering dervish was brought before him. The dervish answered him with a tale: of a jurist who slept with his lamp burning, and rose and demanded of the night why it had stolen his light — and of the judge who fined the flood for wetting his shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Sufi and the Qazi'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The court was silent; the dervish went his way; and the poem's moral is of the jurists who have the letter and not the spirit — 'The fish of the letter is caught in the net of the word, and the man of the sea has gone free.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The King and His Three Sons

region.en: Royal court and artisan quarter (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 王廷與工匠坊（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: Three princes are set to learn a trade; one learns archery, one the manufacture of arrows, one the cure of men. War comes: the archer can no longer use his art, the arrow-maker's wares are taken, and only the healer is wanted. Rumi's moral: the art of healing souls is the trade that no misfortune dearness makes dearer or cheaper.
summary.zh: 三王子奉命習藝：一習射，一習製箭，一習醫人。戰事起：射者技無所用，製箭者貨物被奪，惟醫者受求。魯米之旨：醫治靈魂之藝乃無論窮通皆受求之業。

sensitivity.note: Sufi parable of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A king set his three sons to learn trades. One learned archery, and became the finest bowman of the age; one learned to make arrows, and his wares filled the market; and the third learned to heal the bodies and souls of men. War came, and the archer's art stood idle, and the arrow-maker's stock was seized for the king's men; only the healer was wanted, in war and in peace alike.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The King and his Three Sons'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Rumi's moral is of the science of the saints: the trade that is never dearer for need nor cheaper for peace — the healing of the soul, which every age requires, and which no misfortune can take from the man who has learned it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.

region.en: Konya, shop of the tattooer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科尼亞刺青師鋪（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Masnavi I Ma'navi, Book 1 (composed c. 1258-1264); E. H. Whinfield translation, 1887, public domain

source.work: Jalaluddin Rumi, Masnavi I Ma'navi, translated and abridged by E. H. Whinfield (1887/1898), Book 1

summary.en: A man goes to be tattooed with the figures of a lion on his shoulder, an eagle on his breast, a garland about his thigh. The needle touches his shoulder: 'What are you drawing?' — 'A lion.' 'Begin with the tail, for the shoulder is a tender place.' The needle touches his back: 'What now?' — 'An eagle.' 'Begin at the tail, for the back is tender.' — 'Begin at the thigh.' The artist throws down the needle: 'God never made a man with a tailless lion, a wingless eagle and a headless garland.'
summary.zh: 一人往刺青，欲肩繪獅、胸繪鷹、股繞花環。針及肩：『你畫什麼？』——『獅。』『先從尾開始，肩是嫩處。』針及背：『現在呢？』——『鷹。』『先從尾開始，背是嫩處。』——『從股開始。』刺青師擲針：『主造人從未有無尾之獅、無翼之鷹、無頭之花環。』

sensitivity.note: Sufi anecdote of a living devotional tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Whinfield abridgment.

passages.text: A man went to the tattooer to be marked with a lion on his shoulder, an eagle on his breast and a garland about his thigh. The needle began at the shoulder: 'What art thou drawing?' 'A lion.' 'Begin with the tail, for the shoulder is a tender place.' The needle began at the back: 'What now?' 'An eagle.' 'Begin at the tail, for the back is tender.' 'Then begin at the thigh.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1, 'The Man who was Tattooed'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The artist threw down the needle and said: 'God never made a man with a tailless lion and a wingless eagle and a headless garland.' The moral, says Rumi, is of the dervish who would have the delight of the path without its pain — who will be a lion in the spirit if he may be spared the needle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Rumi, Masnavi (Whinfield 1887), Book 1; not verbatim.
